nameStory: The "Midwestern arrowhead" gets its name from its classic distribution across America's heartland, from the Great Lakes down to the Gulf states. Like all arrowheads, it's named for those distinctive arrow-shaped leaves that look like they could have been fletched by nature itself. The "shortbeak" part of its alternate name refers to the tiny beak-like projection on its fruits being shorter than other arrowhead species.
description: Midwestern arrowhead is an aquatic perennial that loves to wade in shallow water along pond edges and marshy areas. This water-loving plant grows up to about 28 inches tall, sporting the classic arrow-shaped leaves that make arrowheads so recognizable. In summer, it sends up delicate white flowers that seem to float above the water's surface. Though more common in the Midwest as its name suggests, it does pop up in scattered locations throughout New England.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Classic arrowhead shape with three distinct lobes - one pointing forward and two pointing backward like fletching on an arrow. Leaves feel smooth and waxy to the touch, helping them shed water easily.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Pure white flowers with three rounded petals arranged in small clusters along tall stalks. Each flower is about an inch across and has a delicate, papery texture that almost seems translucent in sunlight.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in shallow water or muddy shores with leaves and flower stalks emerging directly from underwater roots. The whole plant has a clean, upright appearance rising from the water.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, flattened fruits clustered in round heads. Each tiny fruit has a short beak-like projection that's noticeably shorter than on other arrowhead species.

habitat: Look for Midwestern arrowhead in shallow water along the edges of ponds, marshes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. It prefers muddy or sandy bottoms where it can anchor its roots while keeping its leaves above the waterline. You'll often find it growing alongside cattails, pickerelweed, and other water-loving plants in these wetland communities.

seasonality.spring: New arrow-shaped leaves begin emerging from the water as temperatures warm, unfurling with a fresh, bright green color.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time with white flowers appearing on tall stalks above the leaves. This is the best time to spot and identify the plant.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed heads develop while leaves may begin to yellow. Seeds ripen and eventually fall into the water.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back completely, leaving only underground roots and tubers to survive until spring.

funFact: Native Americans and early settlers knew arrowheads as "duck potatoes" because the starchy underground tubers were not only a favorite food of waterfowl, but could be harvested and roasted like small potatoes - and they actually taste somewhat like chestnuts when cooked!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with the more common broadleaf arrowhead, but Midwestern arrowhead typically has more slender leaf lobes and those diagnostic short-beaked fruits. Remember: "Midwestern = shorter beak" - the fruit's tiny projection is noticeably more stubby than its relatives.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name suggesting it's only found in the Midwest, this species has a scattered distribution and shows up in isolated pockets throughout New England - likely remnants from when climate conditions were different thousands of years ago. It's much less common here than the abundant broadleaf arrowhead most people know.
compareHints: Compared to the common broadleaf arrowhead, Midwestern arrowhead has more narrow, elongated leaf lobes and distinctly shorter beaks on its fruits. While broadleaf arrowhead is robust and widespread, Midwestern arrowhead tends to be more delicate in appearance and much less common in New England waters.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Broadleaf arrowhead stands out from its relatives by having the widest, most pronounced arrow-shaped leaves in the genus - while grass-leaved arrowhead has narrow, strap-like leaves and slender arrowhead has thin, linear foliage.
Among New England's arrowheads, grass-leaved arrowhead is instantly recognizable by its narrow, grass-like leaves – all other species have distinctly arrow-shaped or oval leaves.
While broadleaf arrowhead has classic arrow-shaped leaves and grass-leaved arrowhead has broader, ribbon-like foliage, slender arrowhead's leaves are so narrow they look like green needles.
Unlike broadleaf arrowhead with its iconic three-pointed arrow leaves, sessile-fruited arrowhead has narrow ovals.
Among New England's arrowheads, arumleaf arrowhead is distinguished by its relatively broad, triangular leaves that are wider than they are long.
Among the arrowhead family, Engelmann's stands out for its extremely narrow leaf lobes and strict preference for acidic water.
Among New England's arrowheads, Spongy Arrowhead is distinguished by its uniquely soft, air-filled leaf stalks - a feature no other local Sagittaria species shares.
Among New England arrowheads, delta arrowhead has broader, more triangular leaves than the common broadleaf arrowhead, and much wider leaves than the grass-like narrow-leaved arrowhead.
Among New England's arrowheads, this species stands out for having the thinnest, most grass-like leaves - much narrower even than grass-leaved arrowhead.

Among New England arrowheads, hooded arrowhead is unique for its curved sepals that hood over the flower petals, while broadleaf arrowhead has flat, open flowers and grass-leaved arrowhead has narrow, grass-like leaves rather than the broad arrow shape.
